subtype_info: Guillain-Barré syndrome associated with Zika virus infection
title: Zika Virus Infection and Guillain-Barré Syndrome in Three Patients from Suriname
case_text: In February 2016, a male in his 40s was admitted to the neurology department of a hospital in Paramaribo, Suriname, because of muscle weakness in the legs, which started 7 days prior to admission. At presentation in the hospital, the patient was unable to walk without help. Two weeks before muscle weakness started he visited the hospital because of urinary retention. Acute myelitis and a cauda syndrome were excluded with an MRI-scan, which showed no abnormalities. The week before muscle weakness started he had an influenza-like syndrome and had a short episode of diplopia. At first physical examination after admission, muscle weakness was observed in predominantly the legs (MRC score 4). Areflexia in both legs and arms was noted. The patient complained of paresthesias and pain in the legs but did not have a sensory level or other signs of myelum involvement. A lumbar puncture was performed 2 days after admission, and a high protein level was found in the CSF (4.4 g/L) while the cell count was slightly increased (32.7 x 106/L). A urine sample, taken at day two after admission, was tested positive for ZIKV RNA with a Ct-value of 35.7. Four days after admission his muscle power improved (MCR score arms 5, legs; proximal 5, distal 4), while the areflexia in arms and legs persisted. Because of the little availability of IVIg in Suriname and because PE is not possible in Suriname, the patient did not received immunotherapy. A motor NCS, performed 15 days after the start of muscle weakness, showed severe decreased NCV and a prolonged DML in all tested nerves. The CMAP was decreased in predominantly the legs (see Table S2 in Supplementary Material). These results were consistent with the demyelinating subtype of GBS. At discharge, 7 days after admission, he was still unable to walk without help due to muscle weakness in the legs. Four months after hospital discharge he was able to walk a few steps without assistance, but he still could not live independently or return to work.

You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Zika Virus
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: Guillain-Barré syndrome associated with Zika virus infection
